title: Employee Directory API
summary: Fix paging and a 500 on bad emails in a Spring Boot people directory, add org-chart endpoints that reject reporting loops, then keep the team listing fast for 50,000 employees.
overview:
You've joined the internal tools team at **Hearthwood**, a mid-sized company. This Spring Boot service is the people directory behind the intranet and the Slack bot: it stores employees (id, name, email, department, title and an optional manager) and the next release adds the org chart.

The codebase is layered the usual way: `controller/` maps HTTP to service calls, `service/` holds the rules (`EmployeeService`, `OrgChartService`), `repository/` keeps everything in memory, `dto/` has the request and response records, and `exception/` turns errors into one JSON shape in `ApiExceptionHandler`.

Start with `README.md`: it is the API contract, with the endpoints, the status codes and the error shape. Then read `EmployeeController`, `EmployeeService` and `EmployeeRepository`. The tests use MockMvc, so they exercise the real controllers, validation and error handling.

phases.title: Missing people and a 500
phases.instructions:
Two reports came in from the intranet team.

> *"The directory list is missing people. With 25 employees in Sales and `page=1&size=10`, I see Person 11 to Person 20 first, and the last page is empty. Nobody can find the first ten."*

> *"When someone mistypes an email on the new-hire form, the form shows 'Something went wrong'. Our logs show the API answered **500**."*

The README is the contract: pages are 1-based, and a malformed email is a `400` with error code `validation_error` and the offending field in `fields`.

**Done when** every test in `Phase1Test` passes. Reproduce each report with a request (or a test) before you change anything.
hints: Both reports are about how the API answers, not about stored data: the employees themselves are fine. Follow each request from the controller into the service.

For the first report, work out by hand which employees `page=1&size=10` should return, then look at how `EmployeeService.list` turns `page` into a starting position. For the second, find what `Emails.requireValid` throws and compare it with the exceptions `ApiExceptionHandler` knows about.

The offset for a 1-based page is `(page - 1) * size`. Make `Emails.requireValid` throw `ValidationFailedException("email", ...)`, which the handler already maps to `400 validation_error` with `fields`.
phases.answer:
**Root cause 1: paging.** `EmployeeService.list` computed the start of the page as `page * size`, which is right for 0-based pages. The README (and `PageResponse`) say pages are 1-based, so page 1 started at index 10, the first ten people were never reachable, and the last page was empty.

**Fix:** `from = (page - 1) * size`, computed in a `long` and clamped to the list size. `page` is already validated to be at least 1.

**Root cause 2: the 500.** `Emails.requireValid` threw a plain `IllegalArgumentException`. No handler matched it, so it fell through to the catch-all `Exception` handler, which answers `500 internal_error`.

**Fix:** throw `ValidationFailedException("email", "must be a well-formed email address")`, an `ApiException` that the handler turns into `400` with the documented body. Bad client input should never be an unchecked exception that nobody maps.

**Verify:** `Phase1Test`, plus a manual `GET /api/employees?page=1&size=10` and a `POST` with `"email": "nope"`.

phases.title: The org chart
phases.instructions:
Build the org-chart endpoints. The controller (`OrgChartController`) and the exception types already exist; the stubs are in `OrgChartService`.

**1. `GET /api/employees/{id}/reports`**: the people who report directly to the employee, as an array sorted by name (ignoring case), then id (`Employee.BY_NAME`). Add `?all=true` to get everyone below them at any depth, with the same sort. Someone with no reports gets `[]`; an unknown id is `404 employee_not_found`.

**2. `GET /api/employees/{id}/chain`**: the management chain as an array: the employee's manager first, then that manager's manager, up to the person at the top. Someone at the top gets `[]`.

**3. `PUT /api/employees/{id}/manager`** with `{"managerId": 7}`, or `{"managerId": null}` to make the employee top-level. `200` with the updated employee. An unknown employee or an unknown `managerId` is `404 employee_not_found`. A manager who is the employee, or who reports to them at any depth, would create a loop: `409 manager_cycle`, and nothing changes.

**Done when** `Phase1Test` and `Phase2Test` pass.
hints: Keep the controller thin; all four stubs are in `OrgChartService`, and `EmployeeRepository.findByManagerId` and `findById` give you what you need.

For all reports, use a queue: start with the employee, and for each id taken from the queue add its direct reports to the result and to the queue. Sort once at the end. For the chain, follow `managerId` upward until it is null.

To detect a cycle, walk up from the proposed manager through `managerId`. If you reach the employee being moved (the manager can be the employee itself), throw `ManagerCycleException`. Do this, and the 404 checks, before saving anything.
phases.answer:
**Reports:** `directReports` is one `findByManagerId` call, sorted with `Employee.BY_NAME`. `allReports` is a breadth-first walk: a queue of ids, calling `findByManagerId` for each one and collecting every employee found; the result is sorted once at the end.

**Chain:** start from the employee's `managerId` and follow it up with `findById` until it is null. Chains are short (the depth of the org chart).

**Assign manager:** look up the employee (404), then the manager (404), then walk up from the manager: if the walk meets the employee, it is a cycle (`409 manager_cycle`), including the case where the manager is the employee itself. Only then `save(employee.withManager(managerId))`. A null manager just clears the link.

Costs: direct reports and each BFS step are O(n) in this repository because `findByManagerId` scans every employee; chain and cycle checks are O(depth). That is fine at a few hundred people, and it is exactly what phase 3 stresses.

phases.title: The org chart at 50,000 people
phases.instructions:
Hearthwood has acquired another company, and the directory now holds about **50,000 employees**. The team page (`GET /api/employees/{id}/reports?all=true`) for a manager with a few hundred people under them has become very slow, and so has the plain direct-reports listing.

Make the org-chart reads production-ready without changing any answer:

- Listing a manager's reports, direct or all, must not scan the whole directory. Looking at employee records one team member at a time is fine; looking at all 50,000 once per manager is not.
- The result must stay identical: the same people, sorted by name (ignoring case), then id.
- The answers must stay right after changes: a new hire shows up under their manager, and someone moved with `PUT .../manager` leaves the old team and joins the new one. Cycle checks keep working.

`EmployeeRepository` counts the records its scanning methods read (`recordsRead()`), and `Phase3Test` uses that counter, so the checks are exact and do not depend on how fast your machine is.

**Done when** all three test classes pass.
hints: Count it: `all=true` calls `findByManagerId` once per person in the team, and each call looks at all 50,000 employees. The cost is team size times company size.
You are asking the same question again and again: "who reports to this manager?" Answer it from a map instead of a scan: manager id to the ids of their direct reports.

Build and maintain that map where employees are saved: in `EmployeeRepository.save`, remove the id from the previous manager's set when the manager changed, then add it to the new manager's set. `findByManagerId` then reads only the employees in the set. The service code can stay as it is.
phases.answer:
**Why phase 2 breaks:** `allReports` calls `findByManagerId` for every employee in the team, and each call scans every employee in the directory. A team of `t` people in a company of `n` costs `O(t * n)`: a few hundred managers times 50,000 records is tens of millions of reads for one request, and the plain `reports` call reads all 50,000 for a handful of results.

**Fix:** keep an index, `Map<Long, Set<Long>>` from manager id to the ids of their direct reports, inside `EmployeeRepository`. `save` updates it: if the employee already existed with a different manager, remove the id from the old set, and add it to the new manager's set when there is one (`save` is synchronized so the two steps stay consistent). `findByManagerId` looks the set up, maps ids to employees and sorts by id, reading only those records.

The breadth-first search in `OrgChartService` is unchanged; it now costs `O(t log t)` for a team of `t` (the final sort) instead of `O(t * n)`. Direct reports cost `O(r)`.

**Verify:** `Phase3Test` checks the order and contents of a seeded team, that listing it reads at most about twice the team size in records, that a new hire and a manager change move between teams correctly, and that cycles are still refused. The cost is a little memory for the index and a little work on every save.

debrief: What did you do to confirm the two phase-1 reports before changing code, and why is `(page - 1) * size` right here while `page * size` would be right in another API? Where else could a 0- versus 1-based mix-up hide?

Walk through how you detect a reporting cycle in `assignManager` and why you validate before saving. What is the cost of that check and of finding all reports, and which edge cases (the employee as their own manager, `null` manager, unknown manager) did you test?

How did you decide an index was the right fix for the team listing, and what must the repository now keep in sync? How did you check that the AI-written change preserved behavior (ordering, manager moves, cycles) and not just the read counts?
